subject: Agriculture
title: Jethro Tull's Seed Drill
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Jethro Tull's Seed Drill.

hook.text: For thousands of years, farmers scattered seed by hand. Most of it landed in the wrong place.

buildup.text: In 1701, Jethro Tull invented a machine that planted seeds in neat rows at a controlled depth.

discovery.text: Row planting wasted less seed and made weeding between rows possible. Yields jumped significantly.

twist.text: Most farmers rejected the seed drill for decades. Hand broadcasting was tradition—and tradition was sacred.

climax.text: It took nearly a century for seed drills to become standard. The best ideas don't always win quickly.

punchline.text: A machine for planting changed farming forever—eventually.

quiz.question: What was the key innovation of Jethro Tull's seed drill?
options: It planted seeds in precise rows at controlled depth

details.summary: Jethro Tull's seed drill, invented around 1701, mechanized seed planting by depositing seeds in neat rows at controlled depths. This topic covers how the seed drill replaced wasteful broadcast sowing and launched the era of mechanized precision farming.
details.whyItMatters: Before the seed drill, farmers scattered seeds by hand, wasting up to 75% of seed and making weeding nearly impossible. Tull's invention improved crop establishment and became the foundation for all modern planting equipment.
takeaways: Broadcast sowing wasted most seeds to birds, poor soil contact, and overcrowding
The seed drill placed seeds at uniform depth and spacing for optimal germination
Row planting enabled horse-drawn hoeing between rows for effective weed control

faq.question: How did Jethro Tull's seed drill work?
faq.answer: The seed drill used a rotating cylinder with grooves to meter seeds into a tube that deposited them into a furrow cut by a coulter. A harrow behind covered the seeds with soil, ensuring uniform depth and spacing in straight rows.

faq.question: Why was the seed drill such an important agricultural invention?
faq.answer: It reduced seed waste from broadcast sowing by up to 75%, improved germination through uniform depth placement, enabled systematic weed control between rows, and was the first step toward the mechanization of planting that continues today.
